questions.title: Memory address
questions.text: Select the **two** statements that explain the principle of memory addressing.

options.content: Main memory is divided into locations, each with its own unique address
The CPU places the address in the MAR and on the address bus to select the location to read or write
Each location's address is stored inside the location together with the data
Memory locations must be read in order, starting from address 0
The address of a location changes each time new data is written to it

scheme.mark_scheme: A, B (1 each; −1 per wrong option)
scheme.explanation: Address and contents are different things; any location can be reached directly (random access).

questions.title: Buses and registers
questions.text: Match each component to its role when memory is accessed.

right.text: Carries the address of the location from the CPU to memory
Carries the data between the CPU and memory
Register holding the address to be accessed
Register holding the data read or to be written

scheme.mark_scheme: Address bus–R1, Data bus–R2, MAR–R3, MDR–R4.

questions.title: Address bus width

questions.title: Address lines
questions.text: How many address lines are needed to address **256 MiB** of byte-addressable memory?

scheme.explanation: 256 MiB = 2⁸ × 2²⁰ = 2²⁸ bytes.

questions.title: Addressing modes
questions.text:
Memory contents: address **50** → 64, address **52** → 17, address **64** → 9. The index register IX = **2**.

Complete the table to show the value loaded into the accumulator by each instruction.

scheme.explanation: Immediate: the value 50. Direct: contents of 50 = 64. Indirect: 50 holds 64, contents of 64 = 9. Indexed: 50 + 2 = 52, contents = 17.

questions.title: Mode descriptions
questions.text: Match each addressing mode to its description.

right.text: The operand is the value to be used
The operand is the address of the value
The operand is the address of a location holding the address of the value
The address is the operand plus the contents of the index register

questions.title: Use of indexed addressing
questions.text: Why is **indexed addressing** useful when processing an array?

options.content: The operand is the value itself, so no memory access is needed
The address is the base address plus the index register, so incrementing IX in a loop lets the same instruction access each element in turn
The operand holds the address of a pointer to the array
The address is worked out relative to the program counter, so the array can be moved

scheme.explanation: A is immediate, C is indirect, D is relative addressing.

questions.title: Stored-program concept
questions.text: Select the **two** statements that describe the stored-program (von Neumann) concept.

options.content: Program instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory, both in binary
Instructions and data are kept in separate memories with separate buses
The CPU fetches instructions one at a time, then decodes and executes them in sequence
To change the program, the computer must be rewired
Data is stored in memory but instructions are stored inside the CPU

scheme.mark_scheme: A, C (1 each; −1 per wrong option)
scheme.explanation: B describes Harvard; D describes early computers such as ENIAC before the stored-program idea.

questions.title: Von Neumann or Harvard
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show which architecture each statement describes.

prefill: Instructions and data share one memory
An instruction and data can be fetched at the same time
Suffers from a bottleneck because of a shared bus
Often used in microcontrollers and signal processors

scheme.explanation: Von Neumann: one shared memory and bus → bottleneck. Harvard: separate memories and buses → instruction and data fetched together; used in microcontrollers and DSPs.

questions.title: Pages needed
questions.text: A program is **18 KiB** and the page size is **4 KiB**. Calculate the amount of memory (in KiB) wasted by internal fragmentation.

questions.title: Segment table
questions.text:
Segment table: segment 0 — base **2000**, limit **500**; segment 1 — base **4500**, limit **1000**; segment 2 — base **8000**, limit **300**.

Complete the physical address for each logical address (segment, offset). Write **error** if the offset is outside the segment.

questions.title: Page size
questions.text: In paging, the pages of a program can have different sizes depending on the program's structure.

scheme.explanation: Pages are a fixed size; segments are variable.

questions.title: Paging vs segmentation
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement describes paging or segmentation.

prefill: Blocks are of a fixed size, e.g. 4 KiB
Blocks follow the logical parts of the program (code, data, stack)
Uses a table of base and limit for each block
Physical address = frame number × block size + offset

scheme.mark_scheme: Blocks are of a fixed size, e.g. 4 KiB – Paging (1); Blocks follow the logical parts of the program (code, data, stack) – Segmentation (1); Causes internal fragmentation – Paging (1); Causes external fragmentation – Segmentation (1); Uses a table of base and limit for each block – Segmentation (1); Physical address = frame number × block size + offset – Paging (1)
scheme.explanation: Paging: fixed, physical, page table, internal fragmentation. Segmentation: variable, logical, segment table (base, limit), external fragmentation.

questions.title: Virtual memory
questions.text:
Complete the description of virtual memory.

Part of [[1]] storage is used as an extension of RAM. Pages that are not needed are moved out to disk and brought back into a free [[2]] when they are needed. If RAM is far too small, the computer spends most of its time moving pages in and out; this is called disk [[3]].

scheme.explanation: Virtual memory relies on paging: single pages are swapped between RAM and the swap file on disk.

questions.title: Virtual machine
questions.text: Which is the best description of a **virtual machine**?

options.content: Using part of the hard disk as if it were extra RAM
Software that emulates a complete computer system, so a guest OS or program runs as if on its own hardware while sharing the host's resources
A computer with more than one CPU core
A program that translates high-level code into machine code before it runs

scheme.explanation: A describes virtual memory — a common confusion.

questions.title: Types of virtual machine
questions.text: Select the **two** examples of a **process** virtual machine.

options.content: Java Virtual Machine running bytecode
VirtualBox running Linux inside Windows
Python interpreter running a script
A cloud server running 20 guest operating systems

scheme.explanation: B and D are system virtual machines.

questions.title: VM advantages and disadvantages
questions.text: A school's IT technician wants to test new software in a virtual machine before installing it on the school computers. Tick (✓) to show whether each point is an advantage or a disadvantage of using a VM.

prefill: A crash or malware in the VM does not harm the host computer
The VM can be restored quickly from a snapshot
Software runs more slowly than on the real hardware
The host needs a lot of RAM, CPU power and storage
Several operating systems can be tested on one computer
If the host fails, every VM on it fails

scheme.mark_scheme: A crash or malware in the VM does not harm the host computer – Advantage (1); The VM can be restored quickly from a snapshot – Advantage (1); Software runs more slowly than on the real hardware – Disadvantage (1); The host needs a lot of RAM, CPU power and storage – Disadvantage (1); Several operating systems can be tested on one computer – Advantage (1); If the host fails, every VM on it fails – Disadvantage (1)
scheme.explanation: Benefits come from isolation, flexibility and sharing hardware; drawbacks from the extra hypervisor layer and shared resources.

questions.title: Memory addressing
questions.text: A computer has a **16-bit** address bus and byte-addressable memory.

parts.title: Principle
parts.text: Explain the principle of memory addressing.

scheme.mark_scheme: Each location has a unique address (1); address placed in MAR / on address bus to access it (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every memory location has a unique address; the CPU puts the address on the address bus to read or write it.

parts.title: Maximum memory
parts.text: Calculate the maximum number of memory locations that can be addressed.

parts.title: Wider bus
parts.text: State the effect of adding **one** extra line to the address bus.

scheme.mark_scheme: The number of addressable locations doubles (1)
scheme.model_answer: The number of addresses doubles.

parts.title: Modes
parts.text:
Memory: address **80** → 95, address **84** → 33, address **95** → 12. Index register IX = **4**.

Complete the value loaded into the accumulator.

parts.title: Direct vs indirect
parts.text: Explain the difference between direct and indirect addressing.

scheme.mark_scheme: Direct: operand is the address of the data (1); indirect: operand is the address of a location holding the address of the data (1)
scheme.model_answer: In direct addressing the operand is the address of the data; in indirect addressing it is the address of a location that holds the address of the data.

questions.title: Memory organisation
questions.text: An operating system manages memory for several programs at once.

parts.title: Stored program
parts.text: Explain the principle of storing programs and data in a von Neumann computer.

scheme.mark_scheme: Instructions and data stored together in the same memory (1); fetched one at a time in sequence over the same bus (1)
scheme.model_answer: Instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory and the CPU fetches instructions one at a time over the same buses.

parts.title: Paging
parts.text: Explain how memory is organised using paging.

scheme.mark_scheme: RAM divided into fixed-size frames (1); program divided into pages of the same size (1); page table maps pages to frames, which need not be contiguous (1)
scheme.model_answer: Physical memory is split into fixed-size frames and each program into pages of the same size; a page table records which frame each page is in, so pages can go anywhere.

parts.title: Translation
parts.text: The page size is **4096 bytes** and page **2** is in frame **5**. Calculate the physical address of logical address **8200**.

parts.title: Segmentation
parts.text: Compare paging with segmentation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any four comparative points (1 each): fixed vs variable size; physical vs logical division; invisible vs visible to programmer; page table vs segment table with base and limit; internal vs external fragmentation; segmentation easier sharing / protection
scheme.model_answer: Pages are fixed size whereas segments vary; paging splits by physical size, segmentation by logical parts such as code and data; paging uses a page table, segmentation a segment table with base and limit; paging gives internal fragmentation, segmentation external.

questions.title: Virtual machines
questions.text: A software company develops a Java application and tests it on Windows, macOS and Linux using virtual machines.

parts.title: Concept
parts.text: Explain the concept of a virtual machine.

scheme.mark_scheme: Software that emulates a computer (1); guest OS / program runs as if on own hardware while sharing host (1)
scheme.model_answer: Software that emulates a whole computer, so a guest OS runs on it as if on real hardware while using the host's resources.

parts.title: JVM
parts.text: Explain how the Java Virtual Machine allows the same program to run on all three operating systems.

scheme.mark_scheme: Java compiled to platform-independent bytecode (1); JVM on each OS translates / interprets bytecode for that machine (1)
scheme.model_answer: Java is compiled to bytecode, which is the same on every platform; each OS has its own JVM that translates the bytecode into that computer's machine code.

parts.title: Testing in VMs
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages for the company of testing in system virtual machines rather than on three separate computers.

scheme.mark_scheme: Up to 2 advantages (1 each): one computer runs all three OSs — cheaper / less space; isolation — crashes do not harm host; snapshots to restore a clean state; easy to copy / share setups. Up to 2 disadvantages (1 each): slower — performance results may not match real hardware; needs much RAM / CPU / storage; hardware access limited; OS licences; host failure stops all
scheme.model_answer: One powerful computer can run all three systems, saving money, and snapshots let testers reset after a crash. However, the VMs run slower so timing tests may be unrealistic, and the host needs a lot of RAM and storage.

questions.title: Memory in a greenhouse controller
questions.text: A farm near Almaty uses a **microcontroller** to control the heating in its greenhouses. The microcontroller has **byte-addressable** main memory and an **18-bit address bus**. Its program stores the latest temperature reading at memory address **120**.

parts.title: Principle of memory addressing
parts.text: Explain the principle of memory addressing.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- main memory is divided into (numbered) locations / cells, each storing a fixed number of bits, e.g. one byte (1)
- each location has its own **unique address** (1)
- the CPU puts the address in the **MAR** / on the **address bus** to select the location; the contents travel on the **data bus** (via the MDR) (1)
Accept: any location can be accessed directly in the same time (random access) (1). (Max 3.)

points.criterion: Memory divided into locations of fixed size
Each location has a unique address
Address sent via MAR / address bus to select it; contents on data bus

scheme.ai_instructions: The third mark needs the address being used (MAR / address bus) to select the location — 'every cell has a number' alone earns only the first two.
scheme.model_answer: Main memory is divided into a large number of locations, each holding a fixed number of bits (here one byte). Every location has its own unique address. To use a location the CPU places its address in the MAR, which puts it on the address bus; memory selects that location, and its contents are transferred along the data bus to or from the MDR. Any location can be reached directly by its address.

parts.title: Maximum memory
parts.text: Calculate the maximum amount of memory, in **KiB**, that this microcontroller can address. Show your working.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- 2¹⁸ = 262 144 addresses × 1 byte = 262 144 bytes (1)
- ÷ 1024 = **256 KiB** (1)
Correct answer with no working: 2 marks.
scheme.model_answer: 18 address lines give 2¹⁸ = 262 144 different addresses. With one byte per location that is 262 144 bytes ÷ 1024 = 256 KiB.

parts.title: Writing a value to memory
parts.text: A new reading, **25**, must be stored at address **120**. Describe how the CPU writes this value to memory.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- address 120 is placed in the **MAR** and the data 25 in the **MDR** (1)
- the address is sent on the **address bus** and the data on the **data bus** (1)
- the control unit sends a **memory write** signal on the **control bus**; 25 is stored at address 120, overwriting the old contents (1)

points.criterion: Address bus and data bus used
Memory write signal on control bus / old value overwritten

scheme.model_answer: The CPU copies the address 120 into the MAR and the value 25 into the MDR. The MAR puts 120 on the address bus and the MDR puts 25 on the data bus. The control unit sends a memory write signal on the control bus, and memory stores 25 in location 120, overwriting the previous reading.

questions.title: Addressing modes
questions.text:
Part of the microcontroller's memory is shown below. The **index register (IX)** contains **4**.

| Address | Contents |
|---|---|
| 50 | 64 |
| 51 | 19 |
| 52 | 7 |
| 54 | 33 |
| 64 | 91 |

The instructions use these addressing modes: `LDM #n` immediate, `LDD n` direct, `LDI n` indirect, `LDX n` indexed. Each instruction loads a value into the accumulator (ACC).

parts.title: Values loaded
parts.text: Complete the table to show the value in the ACC after each instruction is executed on its own.

scheme.mark_scheme:
LDM #50 → 50 (1)
LDD 50 → 64 (1)
LDI 50 → 91 (address 50 holds 64; contents of 64) (1)
LDX 50 → 33 (50 + 4 = 54) (1)
scheme.model_answer: LDM #50 loads the value 50 itself. LDD 50 loads the contents of address 50 = 64. LDI 50: address 50 holds 64, so the contents of address 64 = 91 are loaded. LDX 50: address 50 + IX (4) = 54, contents 33.

parts.title: Indexed addressing for readings
parts.text: The program stores **30** temperature readings in consecutive addresses starting at 200. Explain why indexed addressing is suitable for adding up all the readings.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the address used is the base address (200) **+ the contents of the index register** (1)
- IX is incremented each time round a loop, so the **same instruction** accesses each reading in turn / no need for 30 separate instructions (1)

points.criterion: Increment IX in a loop → same instruction reads each element

scheme.model_answer: With indexed addressing the address is the operand (200) plus the contents of IX. Starting with IX = 0 and adding 1 to IX each time round a loop, the same instruction reads addresses 200, 201, 202 … 229, so all 30 readings are processed without writing 30 separate instructions.

parts.title: Two memory accesses
parts.text: Identify the instruction in part (a) that needs **two** memory accesses to fetch its data.

scheme.model_answer: LDI 50 — it reads address 50 to find the address 64, then reads address 64.

questions.title: Storing programs and data
questions.text: The microcontroller's program and its data are both held in the same main memory. Address **140** contains the bit pattern **0100 0001**.

parts.title: Stored-program concept
parts.text: Explain the **stored-program concept**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- program instructions and data are stored **together in the same main memory**, both in binary (1)
- instructions are **fetched** from memory one at a time, decoded and executed **in sequence** (PC incremented) (1)
- the computer can run a different program by **loading it into memory**, without changing the hardware / rewiring (1)
Accept: instructions and data use the same buses (1). (Max 3.)

points.criterion: Instructions and data in the same memory
Fetched, decoded, executed one at a time in sequence
Program changed by loading software, not rewiring / same buses

scheme.model_answer: In the stored-program (von Neumann) concept, program instructions and data are both stored in binary in the same main memory and use the same buses. The CPU fetches the instructions one at a time from consecutive addresses, decodes and executes them, incrementing the program counter after each fetch. To make the computer do a different job, a different program is simply loaded into memory — no rewiring is needed.

parts.title: Instruction or data?
parts.text: Explain how the CPU decides whether the contents of address 140 are treated as an **instruction** or as **data**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- memory itself does not distinguish them; it depends on how the address is used / context (1)
- if the **program counter** points to 140 during the **fetch** stage it is treated as an instruction; if 140 is used as an **operand** by an instruction it is treated as data (1)

points.criterion: Depends on context / memory cannot tell
PC fetch → instruction; used as operand → data

scheme.model_answer: The bit pattern itself could be the letter A, the number 65 or an instruction — memory does not know which. If the program counter holds 140 during the fetch stage, the word is fetched into the CIR and treated as an instruction; if another instruction uses 140 as its operand, the word is treated as data.

parts.title: Avoiding the bottleneck
parts.text: Some microcontrollers use the **Harvard architecture** instead. Explain how it avoids the **von Neumann bottleneck**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- in von Neumann, instructions and data share one memory and one bus, so they cannot be transferred at the same time / the CPU waits (1)
- Harvard has **separate memories and separate buses** for instructions and data, so the next instruction can be fetched **at the same time** as data is read or written (1)

points.criterion: Bottleneck: shared memory/bus, cannot fetch both at once
Harvard: separate memories and buses → simultaneous access

scheme.model_answer: In the von Neumann architecture instructions and data share the same memory and bus, so an instruction and its data cannot be transferred at the same time and the CPU often waits. The Harvard architecture gives instructions and data separate memories with separate buses, so the next instruction can be fetched while data is being read or written, removing the bottleneck.

questions.title: Paging and segmentation
questions.text:
A school server's operating system manages memory. In one configuration it uses **paging** with a page size of **2 KiB (2 048 bytes)**. The page table of a process is:

| Page | Frame |
|---|---|
| 0 | 4 |
| 1 | 9 |
| 2 | 6 |
| 3 | 1 |

In another configuration it uses **segmentation**. The segment table of a process is:

| Segment | Base | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| 0 (code) | 2 000 | 600 |
| 1 (data) | 5 000 | 900 |
| 2 (stack) | 8 200 | 300 |

parts.title: Translating with paging
parts.text: Calculate the physical address for the logical address **5 000** using the page table. Show your working.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- page number = 5 000 div 2 048 = **2** (1)
- offset = 5 000 − 2 × 2 048 = **904** (1)
- page 2 → frame 6: 6 × 2 048 + 904 = **13 192** (1)
Follow through from a wrong page or offset.
scheme.model_answer: Page = 5 000 div 2 048 = 2; offset = 5 000 − 4 096 = 904. Page 2 is in frame 6, so the physical address = 6 × 2 048 + 904 = 12 288 + 904 = 13 192.

parts.title: Pages for a program
parts.text: A program needs **11 KiB** of memory and is loaded with the 2 KiB pages.

fields.label: Memory unused in the last page (KiB)

scheme.mark_scheme:
6 pages (11 ÷ 2 = 5.5, round up) (1)
6 × 2 − 11 = 1 KiB unused (internal fragmentation) (1)
scheme.model_answer: 11 ÷ 2 = 5.5, so 6 pages are needed (always round up). 6 pages give 12 KiB, so 12 − 11 = 1 KiB of the last page is unused.

parts.title: Translating with segmentation
parts.text: Complete the table using the segment table. Write the physical address, or write **error** if the address is not valid.

scheme.model_answer: (1, 450): 450 < 900, so 5 000 + 450 = 5 450. (2, 300): the offset must be less than the limit 300, so this is an error (segmentation fault). (0, 599): 599 < 600, so 2 000 + 599 = 2 599.

parts.title: Paging vs segmentation
parts.text: Give **two** differences between paging and segmentation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Each difference must refer to both (one-sided: 0). Any two:
- paging uses fixed-size pages whereas segments are variable size (1)
- pages are based on physical size whereas segments follow the logical structure of the program (code, data, stack) (1)
- paging causes internal fragmentation whereas segmentation causes external fragmentation (1)
- page table maps page → frame whereas segment table stores base and limit (1)
- paging is invisible to the programmer whereas segments are visible / easier to share and protect (1)
(Max 2.)
scheme.ai_instructions: Award a mark only for a point that states both sides.
scheme.model_answer: Paging divides memory into fixed-size pages, whereas segmentation uses variable-size segments that follow the logical parts of the program. Paging suffers from internal fragmentation (part of the last page is unused), whereas segmentation suffers from external fragmentation (holes between segments).

questions.title: Virtual memory and virtual machines
questions.text: Aruzhan's laptop has **8 GB** of RAM. She often has a browser, a video editor and a programming environment open at the same time, which together need more than 8 GB. In the computer science lab she also uses **VirtualBox** to run **Linux** on a Windows PC, and she writes **Java** programs that her classmates run on macOS.

parts.title: Virtual memory
parts.text: Explain how **virtual memory** allows Aruzhan to keep all three programs open, and one problem this may cause.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- part of **secondary storage** (disk / SSD) is used as an **extension of RAM** (1)
- pages that are not currently needed are moved out to disk and paged back into a free frame when needed (page fault) (1)
- problem: disk is much slower than RAM; if too much swapping happens the computer spends most of its time moving pages — **disk thrashing** — and slows down (1)

points.criterion: Secondary storage used as extra RAM
Unused pages swapped out / paged in when needed

scheme.model_answer: Virtual memory uses part of the disk or SSD as an extension of main memory. Pages of the programs she is not using at that moment are moved out to the swap file on disk, and when a program needs one of them a page fault occurs and the page is loaded back into a free frame. Because the disk is much slower than RAM, switching between the programs may be slow, and if RAM is far too small the computer may spend most of its time swapping pages (disk thrashing).

parts.title: Concept of a virtual machine
parts.text: Explain the concept of a **virtual machine**, using Aruzhan's use of VirtualBox as an example. Use the terms **host** and **guest**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- software that **emulates a complete computer** (processor, memory, storage, devices) (1)
- the real Windows PC is the **host**; Linux runs as the **guest** OS as if on its own hardware (1)
- the **hypervisor** (VirtualBox) shares the host's hardware between VMs / the guest is **isolated**, so errors in Linux do not harm Windows (1)
scheme.model_answer: A virtual machine is software that emulates a complete computer — processor, memory, disk and devices. VirtualBox (the hypervisor) runs on the real Windows PC, the host, and gives the VM a share of its CPU time, RAM and a virtual disk file. Linux is installed as the guest operating system and runs as if it had its own hardware; it is isolated, so if Aruzhan breaks something in Linux the Windows host is not affected.

parts.title: Java on another platform
parts.text: Explain why Aruzhan's compiled Java program runs on her classmates' macOS computers without being recompiled.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Java is compiled to **bytecode**, not to the machine code of one particular CPU / OS (1)
- each platform has a **Java Virtual Machine** (process VM) that translates / runs the bytecode on that computer (1)

points.criterion: JVM on each platform runs the bytecode

scheme.model_answer: The Java compiler produces bytecode, an intermediate code that is not tied to any processor or operating system. Every platform has its own Java Virtual Machine — a process virtual machine — which translates and runs the same bytecode on that computer, so the program works on macOS without recompiling.

questions.title: Address or contents
questions.text: In the statement "location 30 holds 45", the number 45 is the address of the location.

scheme.explanation: 30 is the address; 45 is the contents stored there.

questions.title: Memory read
questions.text:
Complete the steps of a memory read.

The CPU copies the address into the [[1]]. The address is placed on the [[2]] bus. The control unit sends a memory [[3]] signal on the control bus. Memory places the contents of the location on the [[4]] bus, and they arrive in the [[5]].

scheme.explanation: The address travels CPU → memory on the one-way address bus; contents come back on the two-way data bus.

questions.title: Writing to memory
questions.text: The CPU writes the value 42 to address 6. What happens to the value that was stored at address 6 before?

options.content: It moves to address 7
It is overwritten and lost
It is copied to the MAR
It is added to 42

scheme.explanation: A memory write replaces the old contents of the location.

questions.title: One-way bus
questions.text: Which bus is **one-way**, carrying signals only from the CPU to memory during a memory access?

options.content: Data bus
Address bus
Instruction bus
None — all buses are two-way

scheme.explanation: Memory never sends addresses back; the data bus is two-way.

questions.title: One more address line
questions.text: Adding one more line to the address bus doubles the number of locations the CPU can address.

scheme.explanation: n lines give 2ⁿ addresses, and 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2 × 2ⁿ.

questions.title: Lines for 64 MiB
questions.text: How many address lines are needed for **64 MiB** of byte-addressable memory? Give the number only.

scheme.explanation: Write the size as a power of two: 1 MiB = 2²⁰.

questions.title: 16-bit bus, 4-byte words
questions.text: A computer has a **16-bit** address bus and each location stores **4 bytes**. Calculate the maximum memory in **KiB**.

scheme.explanation: Maximum memory = 2ⁿ × size of each location.

questions.title: Byte-addressable words
questions.text: In byte-addressable memory, a **64-bit** word is stored starting at address **1000**. At which address does the **next** word start? Give the number only.

scheme.mark_scheme: 64 bits = 8 bytes → addresses 1000–1007; the next word starts at 1008.
scheme.explanation: Each byte has its own address, so an 8-byte word uses 8 consecutive addresses.

questions.title: The 4 GB limit
questions.text: A laptop has **8 GB** of RAM but runs a **32-bit** operating system, which can use only about 4 GB. Why?

options.content: Half of the RAM is reserved for the BIOS
32 address bits give only 2³² addresses (4 GiB), so the rest of the RAM has no address the system can form
The data bus is only 32 bits wide, so it can carry only 4 GB at a time
32-bit systems compress memory to save space

scheme.explanation: Installing a 64-bit operating system solves the problem.

questions.title: Choose the addressing mode
questions.text: Match each task to the addressing mode most suited to it.

left.text: Load a simple variable stored at a fixed address
Follow a pointer whose value can change while the program runs
Step through the elements of an array in a loop
Jump back 5 locations in code that may be loaded anywhere in memory

right.text: Immediate
Direct
Indirect
Indexed
Relative

scheme.mark_scheme: Set a counter to 0 – Immediate; Load a simple variable stored at a fixed address – Direct; Follow a pointer whose value can change while the program runs – Indirect; Step through the elements of an array in a loop – Indexed; Jump back 5 locations in code that may be loaded anywhere in memory – Relative. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Memory accesses
questions.text: Complete the table to show how many memory accesses are needed to **get the data** (after the instruction has been fetched) in each addressing mode.

scheme.explanation: Immediate: the value is in the instruction. Direct: read the address. Indirect: read the pointer, then the data — so it is the slowest.

questions.title: Indirect trace
questions.text: Memory: address **40** → 70, address **41** → 22, address **70** → 15. What does `LDI 40` load into the accumulator?

scheme.explanation: Indirect: address 40 holds the address 70; the contents of 70 (15) are loaded. 70 would be direct addressing.

questions.title: Why relative addressing
questions.text: Why is **relative addressing** useful for jumps in a program?

options.content: It is the fastest mode because no memory access is needed
No absolute address appears in the code, so the program still works when it is loaded at a different place in memory
It allows a pointer to be changed while the program runs
It can reach any address in memory, however far away

scheme.explanation: The jump target is the program counter plus an offset; its limit is that it can only reach nearby addresses.

questions.title: Instruction or data?
questions.text: Memory itself does not know whether a word is an instruction or data. How does the CPU decide to treat a word as an **instruction**?

options.content: Instructions are always stored at odd addresses
Instructions have a special flag bit set to 1
The program counter pointed to the word during the fetch stage
Instructions are stored in a separate memory

scheme.explanation: A word is data when an instruction uses its address as an operand. D describes Harvard, not von Neumann.

questions.title: Sequential execution
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

Instructions are stored in consecutive addresses. After each fetch, the program [[1]] is incremented to the next address. Only a [[2]] instruction changes the order, by loading a new address into it.

scheme.explanation: Sequential execution is one of the principles of the stored-program concept.

questions.title: Von Neumann bottleneck
questions.text: What is the **von Neumann bottleneck**?

options.content: The limit on speed caused by instructions and data sharing the same memory and bus, so they cannot be fetched at the same time
The maximum amount of memory set by the width of the address bus
The time taken to rewire a computer to change its program
A program that is too large to fit in RAM

scheme.explanation: Harvard architecture removes it by giving instructions and data separate memories and buses.

questions.title: Separate memories?
questions.text: The von Neumann architecture keeps instructions and data in separate memories.

scheme.explanation: That is Harvard architecture; von Neumann uses one shared memory.

questions.title: Areas of a program in memory
questions.text: Match each area of a running program's memory to what it holds.

right.text: The machine-code instructions
Global variables and constants
Local variables, parameters and return addresses of subroutines
Data created while the program runs, e.g. a list that grows

scheme.mark_scheme: Code area – The machine-code instructions; Data area – Global variables and constants; Stack – Local variables, parameters and return addresses of subroutines; Heap – Data created while the program runs, e.g. a list that grows. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Keeping areas separate lets the OS mark the code area read-only; they are still in the same memory, so this is still von Neumann.

questions.title: Memory management terms
questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: The address as seen by the program, e.g. page + offset
The actual address of the location in RAM
Hardware that translates logical addresses into physical ones
A fixed-size block of physical memory
Maps each page number to the frame that holds it

scheme.mark_scheme: Logical address – The address as seen by the program, e.g. page + offset; Physical address – The actual address of the location in RAM; MMU – Hardware that translates logical addresses into physical ones; Frame – A fixed-size block of physical memory; Page table – Maps each page number to the frame that holds it. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Page and offset
questions.text: The page size is **4 096 bytes**. Complete the page number and offset for each logical address.

scheme.mark_scheme: 9 000: page 2, offset 808; 4 100: page 1, offset 4; 12 500: page 3, offset 212 (1 per row)
scheme.explanation: Page = address div 4 096; offset = address mod 4 096 (the remainder).

questions.title: Physical address
questions.text: The page size is **1 024 bytes**. Page table: page 0 → frame 2, page 1 → frame 4, page 2 → frame 0. Calculate the physical address for logical address **2 100**.

scheme.explanation: Physical address = frame × page size + offset; frame 0 starts at address 0.

questions.title: Invalid page
questions.text: A program has pages 0–3 and the page size is 4 KiB. It uses logical address **17 000** (page 4). What happens?

options.content: The address is translated using frame 4
The MMU raises an error and the OS stops the program
The program is given a fifth page automatically
The address wraps round to page 0

scheme.explanation: This is how paging provides memory protection: a program cannot reach pages it does not own.

questions.title: Pages for 30 KiB
questions.text: A program needs **30 KiB** and the page size is **8 KiB**. How many pages does it need? Give the number only.

scheme.explanation: You cannot have part of a page, so always round up; the unused 2 KiB is internal fragmentation.

questions.title: Segment translation
questions.text: Segment 3 has base **12 000** and limit **800**. Calculate the physical address for logical address **(3, 799)**.

scheme.explanation: Check offset < limit, then physical = base + offset.

questions.title: Offset equal to limit
questions.text: A segment has limit 400. The logical address (segment, offset 400) is valid because the offset is not greater than the limit.

scheme.explanation: The offset must be **less than** the limit; offsets run 0–399, so 400 is one byte past the end → error.

questions.title: Benefits of segmentation
questions.text: Select the **three** advantages of segmentation.

options.content: The code segment can be marked read-only and executable
Whole segments, such as a shared library, can be shared between programs
Segments match the logical structure of the program
It causes no external fragmentation
Every segment is exactly 4 KiB, so allocation is simple

scheme.mark_scheme: A, B, C (1 each; −1 per wrong option)
scheme.explanation: Segmentation causes external fragmentation (holes between segments); fixed-size blocks describe paging.

questions.title: Page fault
questions.text:
Complete the description of what happens on a page fault.

The program uses a page that is not in RAM, so a page [[1]] occurs. If no frame is free, the OS chooses a [[2]] page — usually the least recently used — and writes it to disk if it was changed. It reads the required page from the [[3]] into the frame, updates the page [[4]], and the instruction is [[5]].

scheme.explanation: A page fault is an interrupt handled by the OS; the program does not notice except for a short delay.

questions.title: Disk thrashing
questions.text: What is **disk thrashing**?

options.content: Damage to a hard disk caused by overheating
The computer spends most of its time moving pages between RAM and disk instead of running programs
Deleting the swap file to free disk space
Splitting a program into fixed-size pages

scheme.explanation: It happens when RAM is far too small for the programs that are open.

questions.title: Curing thrashing
questions.text: Select the **two** actions that reduce disk thrashing.

options.content: Add more RAM
Make the swap file larger
Close programs / run fewer programs at once
Use smaller pages
Defragment the hard disk

scheme.mark_scheme: A, C (1 each; −1 per wrong option)
scheme.explanation: Thrashing is caused by too little RAM for the open programs; a bigger swap file only allows more swapping.

questions.title: Benefits of virtual memory
questions.text: Select the **two** benefits of virtual memory.

options.content: Programs larger than physical RAM can run
Disk access is faster than RAM access
More programs can be open at the same time
It removes the need for a page table
It makes the CPU's clock faster

scheme.mark_scheme: A, C (1 each; −1 per wrong option)
scheme.explanation: Its drawback is speed: disk is thousands of times slower than RAM.

questions.title: Two different ideas
questions.text: Virtual memory and a virtual machine are two names for the same thing.

scheme.explanation: Virtual memory uses disk as an extension of RAM; a virtual machine is software that imitates a whole computer.

questions.title: Host, guest and hypervisor
questions.text: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: The real, physical computer on which the VMs run
The operating system or program running inside the VM
Software that creates and runs VMs and shares the real hardware between them
A large file on the host that the VM uses as its hard disk

scheme.mark_scheme: Host – The real, physical computer on which the VMs run; Guest – The operating system or program running inside the VM; Hypervisor – Software that creates and runs VMs and shares the real hardware between them; Virtual disk – A large file on the host that the VM uses as its hard disk. One mark per correct match.
scheme.explanation: Examples of hypervisors: VirtualBox, VMware, Hyper-V, KVM.

questions.title: The Java Virtual Machine
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

A Java program is compiled into an intermediate code called [[1]]. Each platform has its own [[2]], which translates this code into the [[3]] code of that computer while the program runs. So the same compiled program runs on any computer — this is called platform [[4]].

scheme.explanation: The JVM is a process virtual machine: it runs one program, not a whole OS.

questions.title: System or process VM
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement describes a system VM or a process VM.

prefill: Emulates a complete computer so a whole guest OS can be installed
Runs a single application, e.g. Java bytecode
Starts when the program starts and ends when it ends
Used to run Linux inside Windows with VirtualBox
Lets a data centre run dozens of virtual servers on one machine

scheme.mark_scheme: Emulates a complete computer so a whole guest OS can be installed – System VM (1); Runs a single application, e.g. Java bytecode – Process VM (1); Starts when the program starts and ends when it ends – Process VM (1); Used to run Linux inside Windows with VirtualBox – System VM (1); Main purpose is platform independence – Process VM (1); Lets a data centre run dozens of virtual servers on one machine – System VM (1)

questions.title: Opening a suspicious file
questions.text: A technician opens a suspicious email attachment inside a virtual machine. Which property of VMs protects the real computer?

options.content: Platform independence
Isolation — the guest cannot see or damage the host
Virtual memory
Relative addressing

scheme.explanation: If the file is malware, only the VM is affected; it can be deleted or restored from a snapshot.

questions.title: Host failure
questions.text: If the physical host computer fails, only one of the virtual machines running on it is affected.

scheme.explanation: All VMs share the host, so if it fails every VM on it fails.

questions.title: Offset bits
questions.text: The page size is **4 KiB**. How many of the lowest bits of a logical address form the **offset**? Give the number only.

scheme.explanation: The remaining higher bits form the page number, so the split is very fast in hardware.

summary: How main memory is organised into addressed locations, how the address bus width sets the number of addresses, addressing modes (immediate, direct, indirect, indexed, relative), the stored-program (von Neumann) principle and Harvard architecture, memory organisation by pages and segments with address translation, virtual memory, and virtual machines.

blocks.text: Main memory as a list of numbered locations

blocks.content: **Main memory (RAM)** holds the programs that are running and the data they are working on. Physically it is a huge grid of tiny storage cells, but logically the CPU sees it as one very long **list of storage locations**, numbered from **0** upwards. Each location holds a fixed amount of data — in almost all modern computers **one byte** (8 bits) — and each has its own number, its **address**. The address is like a house number on a long street: the house number does not tell you who lives there, it only tells you **where** to go. In the same way, the address of a location is not the data; it is the **number of the place** where the data is kept.

This idea is the **principle of memory addressing**: memory is divided into locations, **every location has a unique address**, and the CPU can **read or write any location directly** by giving its address. Because any address can be reached in the same time, no matter where it is, main memory is called **random-access memory** — the CPU does not have to read locations 0, 1, 2… in order to reach location 5 000, as it would with a tape.

A **unique number that identifies one storage location** in main memory. The CPU uses the address to select the location it wants to **read from** or **write to**. The address and the contents of a location are two different things.
A unit of main memory that stores a **fixed number of bits** — usually **one byte** — and is identified by **one address**.

blocks.text: The buses and registers that use the address

blocks.content: The CPU and main memory are joined by three groups of wires, the **system buses**. Each has a clear job in memory addressing:

items: The **address bus** carries the **address** of the location from the CPU to memory. It is **one-way** (CPU → memory): memory never sends addresses back.
The **data bus** carries the **contents** — the data or instruction — between CPU and memory. It is **two-way**: data goes to memory when writing and to the CPU when reading.
The **control bus** carries **control signals**, for example *memory read*, *memory write* and the **clock** signal, so memory knows what to do with the address it receives.

blocks.content: Inside the CPU two special registers sit at the ends of these buses. The **Memory Address Register (MAR)** holds the address of the location that is about to be used; its contents are placed on the address bus. The **Memory Data Register (MDR)** — also called the memory buffer register — holds the data that has just been read from memory, or that is about to be written to it; it is connected to the data bus.

blocks.caption: The CPU selects a location by putting its address on the address bus; the contents travel on the data bus

blocks.title: Reading from memory (for example, loading the contents of address 3)
items: The CPU copies the address **3** into the **MAR**.
The MAR puts the address on the **address bus**; memory decodes it and selects location 3.
The control unit sends a **memory read** signal on the **control bus**.
Memory places the contents of location 3 (0000 0101) on the **data bus**.
The data arrives in the **MDR**, from where it is copied to the register that needs it (e.g. the accumulator).

blocks.title: Writing to memory (for example, storing 42 at address 6)
items: The CPU copies the address **6** into the **MAR** and the data **42** into the **MDR**.
The address goes on the **address bus** and the data on the **data bus**.
The control unit sends a **memory write** signal.
Memory stores 42 in location 6; the **old contents are overwritten** and lost.

blocks.content: A **word** is the number of bits the CPU handles as one unit — the size of its registers and usually the width of the data bus, for example 16, 32 or 64 bits. Memory can be addressed in two ways. In **byte-addressable** memory every **byte** has its own address, so a 64-bit (8-byte) word occupies 8 consecutive addresses, for example 1000–1007, and the next word starts at 1008. Almost all modern computers are byte-addressable, because text characters and many other data items are one byte long and must be reachable individually. In **word-addressable** memory each address holds a **whole word**; this was common in older computers and is still used in some digital signal processors. With the same number of addresses, word-addressable memory can hold more data, but single bytes cannot be reached directly.

blocks.text: How the address bus width limits the memory

blocks.content: Each line (wire) of the address bus carries one bit of the address. With **n lines** the CPU can form **2ⁿ different binary numbers**, so it can select **2ⁿ different locations** — no more. This is why the width of the address bus sets the **maximum amount of memory** the CPU can use. **Adding one line doubles** the number of addresses, because every existing address can now be combined with a 0 or a 1 in the new bit.
The **maximum memory a CPU can address**: **2ⁿ × size of each location**, where **n** is the width of the address bus in bits. With byte-addressable memory, this is simply **2ⁿ bytes**.

blocks.title: Address bus width and maximum addressable memory (1 byte per location)
rows: In practice CPUs use about 48 lines → 256 TiB

blocks.title: Worked example — address bus calculations
blocks.content:
1. A computer has a **24-bit** address bus and each location holds a **2-byte** word. Maximum memory = 2²⁴ × 2 = 16 777 216 × 2 = 33 554 432 bytes = **32 MiB**.
2. How many address lines are needed for **256 MiB** of byte-addressable memory? 256 MiB = 2⁸ × 2²⁰ = 2²⁸ bytes → **28 lines**.
3. A school's old laptop runs a 32-bit operating system and has 8 GB of RAM fitted. It can use only **4 GiB**, because 32 address bits give only 2³² addresses — the rest of the RAM has no address the system can form. Installing a 64-bit operating system solves the problem.

Memory addressing is what makes a general-purpose computer possible. Because every location can be reached **directly** by its address, a program can keep thousands of variables and jump straight to any one of them; the CPU can fetch the next instruction from wherever the program counter points; and the operating system can place different programs in different **ranges of addresses** and keep them apart. Every topic in the rest of this lesson — addressing modes, the stored-program concept, paging and segmentation — is a way of **using or translating addresses**.

A machine-code instruction has two parts. The **opcode** says **what to do** (load, add, store, jump…). The **operand** gives the information the instruction works on. But an operand is just a number — 30, for example — and the CPU needs to know **what that number means**: is it the value itself, the address of the value, or something from which the address must be worked out? The **addressing mode** tells it. In assembly language the mode is often built into the opcode (LDM, LDD, LDI, LDX) or shown by a symbol such as **#** for an immediate value.

The method the CPU uses to **interpret the operand** of an instruction in order to find the **data** (or the address) it needs — for example as the value itself, as an address, or as an address to which an index is added.

items: **Immediate addressing** — the operand **is the actual value** to be used. `LDM #30` loads the number 30 into the accumulator. No memory access is needed to fetch the data, so it is the **fastest** mode, but the value is fixed when the program is written. Used for **constants**: setting a counter to 0, adding 1, comparing with 100.

**Direct addressing** — the operand is the **address** of the value. `LDD 30` goes to location 30 and loads whatever is stored there. One memory access is needed. Used for **simple variables** stored at a fixed address. Its limit: the address must fit into the operand field — an 8-bit operand can only reach addresses 0–255.

**Indirect addressing** — the operand is the address of a location that **holds the address** of the value. `LDI 30` reads location 30, finds (say) 45 there, and then loads the contents of location 45. Two memory accesses are needed, so it is slower, but it allows **pointers** (the address of the data can be changed while the program runs) and reaching addresses **larger than the operand field** could hold, because a whole memory word can store the address.

**Indexed addressing** — the address is the operand **plus the contents of the index register (IX)**. `LDX 30` with IX = 3 loads from address 33. Increasing IX by 1 each time round a loop makes the same instruction read 30, 31, 32… — perfect for stepping through an **array** or a list of marks.

**Relative addressing** — the address is worked out **relative to the current instruction**, i.e. the operand is added to the **program counter**. `JMR 5` jumps five locations forward from where the program is. Because no absolute address appears in the code, the program still works when the operating system loads it at a **different place** in memory — the code is **relocatable**. Used mainly for jumps in loops and IF statements.

blocks.title: Worked example — what is loaded into the accumulator?
blocks.content:
Memory: address **30** → 45, **31** → 12, **33** → 60, **45** → 78. Index register **IX = 3**.

| Instruction | Mode | Working | ACC |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LDM #30` | Immediate | the value 30 itself | **30** |
| `LDD 30` | Direct | contents of address 30 | **45** |
| `LDI 30` | Indirect | address 30 holds 45 → contents of address 45 | **78** |
| `LDX 30` | Indexed | 30 + 3 = 33 → contents of address 33 | **60** |

If the program then executes `INC IX` (IX becomes 4) and `LDX 30` again, it loads the contents of address 34 — the next element of the array.

blocks.title: Worked example — adding up the marks of a class with indexed addressing
blocks.content: The marks of 25 students are stored in addresses 200–224. A program sets **IX = 0** and **ACC = 0** (immediate addressing: `LDM #0`). In a loop it executes `ADD` with indexed addressing on base address 200, so the first time it adds the contents of 200 + 0, then IX is incremented and the same instruction adds 200 + 1, 200 + 2 … up to 200 + 24. After 25 passes the accumulator holds the total. Without indexed addressing the programmer would need 25 different instructions, one for each address. The loop's jump back to its start uses **relative** addressing, so the whole program can be loaded anywhere in memory.

blocks.content: The earliest electronic computers, such as ENIAC (1945), were programmed by **rewiring**: to change the program, engineers moved cables and switches, which could take days. In 1945 John von Neumann described a different design, which every ordinary computer still follows today. Its central idea is that **the program itself is data**: the instructions are coded as binary numbers and stored in **the same main memory** as the data they work on. To run a different program, you do not touch the hardware — you simply **load a different set of instructions into memory**.

**Program instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory**, both in binary. The CPU **fetches the instructions one at a time** from memory, **decodes** and **executes** them, using the **same buses** for instructions and data.
The key principles, each of which can be asked in an exam:

items: **One memory for instructions and data.** Both are sequences of bits stored at addresses. A location that contains 0100 0001 could be the letter "A", the number 65 or an instruction — memory itself does not know which.

**The CPU tells instructions from data by context.** A word is treated as an instruction because the **program counter (PC)** pointed to it during the **fetch** stage. It is treated as data when an instruction refers to its address as an operand.

**Sequential execution.** Instructions are stored in consecutive addresses and executed **one after another**: after each fetch the PC is **incremented** to the next address. Only a **jump/branch** instruction changes the order, by loading a new address into the PC.

**Programs can be changed easily.** Because programs live in memory, a computer becomes a word processor, a game or a compiler simply by loading different software. A program can even **produce another program** as its output — this is exactly what a compiler does.

  C --> D[PC incremented to point to the next instruction]

blocks.text: Where programs and data are kept in memory

blocks.content: When a program runs, the operating system gives it a range of addresses and organises them into areas. The **code** area holds the machine-code instructions. The **data** area holds global variables and constants. The **stack** stores local variables, parameters and return addresses while subroutines run, and the **heap** holds data created while the program runs (for example a list that grows). Keeping instructions and data in separate **areas** does not break the von Neumann idea — they are still in the same memory and reached over the same buses — but it lets the operating system mark the code area as **read-only**, so that a bug or a virus cannot overwrite the instructions. This division into logical areas is the basis of **segmentation**, studied in the next lesson.

blocks.title: Worked example — a tiny program and its data in the same memory
blocks.content:
A program that adds two numbers is loaded starting at address 100. Its data is stored at addresses 200–202.

| Address | Contents | Instruction or data? |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | `LDD 200` | instruction — load the first number |
| 101 | `ADD 201` | instruction — add the second number |
| 102 | `STO 202` | instruction — store the result |
| 103 | `END` | instruction — stop |
| 200 | 17 | data |
| 201 | 25 | data |
| 202 | 42 (after running) | data — the result |

The PC starts at 100. Fetches take place from 100, 101, 102, 103, so those words are treated as instructions. Addresses 200–202 are only ever used as **operands**, so they are treated as data. If, by mistake, a jump sent the PC to 200, the CPU would try to decode 17 as an instruction — showing that memory itself does not distinguish code from data.

Sharing one memory and one set of buses is simple and flexible, but it has a cost. An instruction and the data it needs **cannot be transferred at the same time**, because they would both need the data bus. In addition, the CPU is many times faster than main memory, so it often has to **wait** for the next instruction or data item to arrive. This limit on performance is called the **von Neumann bottleneck**. Modern computers reduce it with **cache memory** (small, very fast memory inside the CPU that keeps recently used instructions and data), **pipelining** (fetching the next instruction while the current one is executing), wider data buses and higher bus speeds.
The **limit on speed** caused by instructions and data **sharing the same memory and bus**: they cannot be fetched at the same time, so the CPU often waits for memory.

The **Harvard architecture** removes the bottleneck by giving instructions and data **separate memories with separate buses**. While one instruction is being executed and its data is read over the data bus, the next instruction can already be fetched over the instruction bus. The price is a more complex and expensive design, and the split of memory between code and data is **fixed** — free space in the instruction memory cannot be used for data. Harvard architecture is used where speed and predictability matter more than flexibility: **microcontrollers** (in a washing machine, a car's ABS, an Arduino), **digital signal processors** that process sound and video in real time, and inside modern CPUs, where the **level 1 cache** is split into an instruction cache and a data cache, while main memory stays von Neumann (a "modified Harvard" design).

blocks.title: Exam-style questions with model answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain the principle of memory addressing. [3]**
Main memory is divided into locations, each storing a fixed number of bits (e.g. one byte) (1); each location has a **unique address** (1); the CPU places the address in the **MAR** and on the **address bus** to select the location, and the contents are transferred on the **data bus** (1).

**Q: A computer has a 20-bit address bus and 1 byte per location. Calculate the maximum memory it can address. [2]**
2²⁰ = 1 048 576 addresses (1) × 1 byte = **1 MiB** (1).

**Q: Explain the difference between direct and indirect addressing. [2]**
In **direct** addressing the operand is the **address of the data** (1); in **indirect** addressing the operand is the address of a location that **contains the address** of the data (1).

**Q: Explain why indexed addressing is useful when processing an array. [2]**
The address = base address + contents of the **index register** (1); incrementing IX in a loop lets the **same instruction** access each element in turn (1).

**Q: Explain the stored-program concept. [3]**
Instructions and data are stored in the **same memory** in binary (1); instructions are **fetched one at a time**, decoded and executed in sequence (1); the program can be changed by loading a different program into memory, without changing the hardware (1).

**Q: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of the Harvard architecture compared with von Neumann. [2]**
Advantage: an instruction and data can be fetched **at the same time** (separate buses), so it is faster (1). Disadvantage: more complex / expensive; the memory split between code and data is **fixed** (1).

- "Explain" questions on memory addressing need the **buses or registers**, not just "every cell has a number".
- In calculations, show **2ⁿ** and the unit conversion; an answer like "1 MB" alone may get only 1 mark.
- When comparing architectures, use **comparative** words ("whereas", "faster because…") rather than two separate descriptions.

blocks.text: Why memory has to be organised

blocks.content: A modern computer runs many programs at once: a browser, a messenger, a music player and the operating system itself. All of them need space in main memory, programs start and finish at different times, and they need different amounts of memory. The **operating system's memory manager** must decide **where** each program goes, keep programs from **interfering** with each other, and make good use of the free space. The simplest approach — giving each program one **contiguous** (continuous) block of addresses — quickly fails: as programs finish, the free memory breaks up into small separate holes, and a new program may not fit into any single hole even though the total free memory is large enough. This waste is called **external fragmentation**. Two methods of organising memory solve the problem in different ways: **paging** and **segmentation**.

Both methods depend on the difference between two kinds of address. A **logical (virtual) address** is the address the program uses — each program believes it starts at address 0. A **physical address** is the real address of a location in RAM. While the program runs, every logical address is **translated** into a physical address by hardware called the **memory management unit (MMU)**, using tables that the operating system keeps.

A **logical address** is an address as seen by the program (relative to its own start, e.g. page + offset). A **physical address** is the actual address of the location in main memory. The **memory management unit (MMU)** translates logical addresses into physical ones.

A method of memory organisation in which **physical memory is divided into fixed-size blocks called frames**, and each program's **logical memory is divided into blocks of the same size called pages**. Any page can be loaded into **any free frame**, and a **page table** records which frame holds each page.

With paging, the operating system no longer needs one large hole for a program. It cuts the program into pages — typically **4 KiB** each — and puts each page into whatever frame is free, anywhere in RAM. The pages of one program can be scattered, out of order, between the pages of other programs. The program does not notice, because each program has its own **page table**: for every page number it gives the **frame number** where that page is stored at the moment (and a *valid* bit saying whether the page is in RAM at all).

A table kept by the operating system for each process that **maps each page number to the frame number** where the page is stored in physical memory, together with status bits (e.g. whether the page is in RAM).

blocks.content: Every logical address is split into two parts: the **page number** (which page) and the **offset** (how far into the page). Because pages and frames are the same size, the offset is the same in both — only the page number has to be changed into a frame number. If the page size is a power of two, the split is very fast in hardware: with 4 KiB = 2¹² byte pages, the lowest **12 bits** of the address are the offset and the remaining bits are the page number.

blocks.title: How to translate a logical address with paging
items: **Page number** = logical address **div** page size (whole-number division).
**Offset** = logical address **mod** page size (the remainder).
Look up the page number in the **page table** to find the **frame number**.
**Physical address = frame number × page size + offset.**
If the page table says the page is **not in RAM**, a **page fault** occurs and the OS must load the page first (see virtual memory).

blocks.title: Worked example — translating addresses (page size 4 KiB = 4 096 bytes)
blocks.content:
The page table of a program is: page 0 → frame 3, page 1 → frame 5, page 2 → frame 1, page 3 → frame 6.
1. Logical address **8 200**: page = 8 200 div 4 096 = **2**; offset = 8 200 − 2 × 4 096 = **8**. Page 2 is in frame **1**. Physical address = 1 × 4 096 + 8 = **4 104**.
2. Logical address **5 000**: page = **1**, offset = 5 000 − 4 096 = **904**. Page 1 → frame 5. Physical = 5 × 4 096 + 904 = **21 384**.
3. Logical address **100**: page **0**, offset **100**. Page 0 → frame 3. Physical = 12 288 + 100 = **12 388**.
4. Logical address **17 000**: page = 17 000 div 4 096 = **4**. The program has only pages 0–3, so this address is **invalid** — the MMU raises an error and the OS stops the program. This is how paging also provides **memory protection**.

blocks.title: Worked example — how many pages, and how much is wasted?
blocks.content: A program needs **18 KiB** and the page size is **4 KiB**. 18 ÷ 4 = 4.5, so it needs **5 pages** (always round **up** — you cannot have half a page). Five pages provide 20 KiB, so the last page has 20 − 18 = **2 KiB unused**. This waste **inside** the last page is **internal fragmentation**. On average a program wastes half a page, so smaller pages waste less memory but need bigger page tables.

Paging removes external fragmentation completely: every free frame is the right size for any page, so if there are enough free frames, the program fits, no matter where they are. It makes loading and removing programs simple, gives each program its own protected address space, and — most importantly — makes **virtual memory** possible, because a single page can be moved between RAM and disk without moving the rest of the program. Its costs are **internal fragmentation**, the memory used by **page tables** (one per process), and the extra time for a table look-up on every memory access. To avoid doubling every access time, the MMU keeps recently used translations in a small fast cache called the **translation lookaside buffer (TLB)**. Finally, pages are cut by **size, not by meaning**: one function may be split across two pages, and one page may contain both code and data, which makes **sharing** and **protecting** logical parts of a program harder.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages of paging
rows: Pages need **not be contiguous** — any free frame can be used
**Internal fragmentation** — the last page is usually partly empty
Every process needs a **page table**, which uses memory
Easy allocation: just find free frames
Each access needs a table look-up (sped up by the **TLB**)
Each process has its own protected address space
Pages ignore the **logical structure** — a function or array may be split
Makes **virtual memory** easy — single pages can be swapped
Sharing or protecting whole modules is less natural

blocks.text: Segmentation: blocks that follow the program's structure

blocks.content: Paging cuts a program into equal pieces without looking at what is inside. **Segmentation** takes the opposite view: a program is made of **logical parts** — the main code, each library or module, global data, the stack — and these parts have **different sizes**. Segmentation gives each part its own **segment** of exactly the size it needs. The programmer (or the compiler) can see the segments, and an address is written as a pair **(segment number, offset)**: "byte 250 of the data segment".

A method of memory organisation in which a program is divided into **variable-size logical blocks called segments** (e.g. code, data, stack, individual modules). Each address is **segment number + offset**, and a **segment table** stores each segment's **base address** and **limit**.

For each segment, the **base** is the **physical address where the segment starts** in RAM and the **limit** is its **length**. A logical address (s, d) is valid only if **d < limit**; then the physical address = **base + d**.

blocks.title: How to translate a logical address with segmentation
items: Split the logical address into **segment number s** and **offset d**.
Look up segment s in the **segment table** to find its **base** and **limit**.
Check **d < limit**. If not, the address is outside the segment → **error (segmentation fault)**; the program is stopped.
If the check passes, **physical address = base + d**.

blocks.content:
| Logical address | Check | Physical address |
|---|---|---|
| (1, 250) | 250 < 1 200 ✓ | 3 000 + 250 = **3 250** |
| (0, 399) | 399 < 400 ✓ (the last byte of the code) | 1 000 + 399 = **1 399** |
| (2, 0) | 0 < 500 ✓ | **6 000** (the first byte of the stack) |
| (0, 400) | 400 is **not** < 400 ✗ | **error** — one byte past the end of the code |
| (2, 600) | 600 ≥ 500 ✗ | **segmentation fault** — the program tried to go outside its stack |

The limit check is what gives segmentation its strong **protection**: a program cannot read or overwrite memory outside its own segments.

Because segments match the **logical structure** of the program, the operating system can treat each part differently. The **code** segment can be marked **read-only and executable**, the **data** segment **read/write but not executable**, so an attempt to overwrite instructions or to run data as code is stopped. Whole segments can be **shared**: if thirty students run the same text editor on a school server, one copy of its code segment can be shared by all thirty processes, each with its own data segment. A segment can also **grow** (for example the stack) without affecting the others. There is **no internal fragmentation**, because each segment is exactly as large as it needs to be.

The weakness is the other kind of fragmentation. Segments of different sizes are loaded and removed over time, leaving **holes of different sizes** between them in RAM. A new 2 KiB segment may not fit into any of several 1 KiB holes, even though there is enough free memory in total — **external fragmentation**. The operating system then has to **compact** memory (move segments together), which takes time. Allocation is also harder, because the OS must search for a hole big enough for each segment. Many real systems therefore **combine** the two methods — **segmentation with paging**: a program is divided into logical segments, and each segment is then divided into pages, giving the protection of segments and the easy allocation of pages.

rows: **Variable** — each segment as large as needed
**Logical** structure of the program (code, data, stack, modules)
No — done by the OS and hardware
Easier — whole code or data segments can be shared or protected
Harder — must find a hole big enough

blocks.text: Using secondary storage as an extension of RAM

blocks.content: Main memory is limited, but users open more and more programs, and some programs are larger than the whole of RAM. **Virtual memory** solves this by using part of **secondary storage** (the hard disk or SSD) **as if it were extra main memory**. The idea relies on paging: a program does not need all its pages in RAM at the same time — only the pages it is using **right now** (the code it is executing and the data it is working on). The other pages can wait on the disk, in an area called the **swap file** or **page file**.

A memory-management technique in which an area of **secondary storage** is used **as an extension of main memory**. Pages that are not currently needed are **moved out to disk (paged out)** and brought back into a free frame (**paged in**) when they are needed, so programs can use more memory than the physical RAM.

An interrupt that occurs when a program uses a page that is **not currently in RAM**. The operating system finds the page on disk, loads it into a free frame (removing another page if necessary) and updates the page table; the program then continues.

blocks.title: What happens on a page fault
items: The program uses an address; the MMU looks up its page and finds that the page is **not in RAM** → **page fault**.
The OS finds a **free frame**. If none is free, it chooses a **victim page** — usually one that has not been used for the longest time (least recently used) — and writes it to disk if it was changed.
The OS **reads the required page** from the disk into the frame.
The **page table** is updated: the page is now valid and in that frame.
The instruction that caused the fault is **restarted** and now succeeds.

blocks.text: Benefits and the problem of disk thrashing

blocks.content: Virtual memory lets programs **larger than RAM** run, lets **more programs** be open at once, and frees programmers from worrying about how much RAM a particular computer has. Its weakness is **speed**: even a fast SSD is thousands of times slower than RAM. As long as most accesses go to pages already in RAM, the computer feels normal. But if RAM is far too small for the programs that are open, the OS keeps removing pages that are needed again a moment later. The computer then spends most of its time **moving pages in and out** instead of running programs: the disk light stays on, the mouse stutters and programs freeze. This is **disk thrashing**. The cure is to **add more RAM**, close programs, or run fewer programs at once.

blocks.title: Worked example — a student laptop with 4 GB of RAM
blocks.content: Daniyar has 4 GB of RAM. Windows uses 1.5 GB, a browser with twenty tabs 2 GB, an IDE 1 GB and a video call 0.8 GB — 5.3 GB in total. Without virtual memory the last program could not start. With virtual memory, pages of the tabs he is not looking at are paged out to the SSD, so everything runs. When he switches to an old tab there is a short delay while its pages are paged in. When he also starts a game needing 3 GB, nearly every page the game needs pushes out a page another program will soon need — the laptop starts **thrashing** and becomes almost unusable. Closing the browser or upgrading to 16 GB of RAM fixes the problem.

blocks.title: Virtual memory: benefits and drawbacks
rows: Programs **larger than physical RAM** can run
Disk is much **slower** than RAM — paging in causes delays
**More programs** can be open at the same time
**Disk thrashing** if RAM is far too small
Each program gets a large, private **logical address space**
Uses space on the disk for the swap file
RAM is used only for pages actually needed
Heavy swapping can wear out SSDs faster

blocks.text: The concept of a virtual machine

blocks.content: Paging and virtual memory already give each program the **illusion** of having a large memory of its own. A **virtual machine** takes the same idea much further: it gives software the illusion of having a **whole computer** of its own — processor, memory, storage, network card and screen — when in fact it is running inside software on a real computer and sharing its hardware with other virtual machines.

**Software that emulates (imitates) a complete computer system** — processor, memory, storage and devices — so that an operating system or program runs **as if on its own hardware**, while actually sharing the resources of a real **host** computer.

items.title: Host
items.content: The **real, physical computer** with its hardware (and usually its own operating system) on which the virtual machines run.

items.title: Guest
items.content: The **operating system or program running inside the VM**. It "thinks" it has the hardware to itself.

items.title: Hypervisor (virtual machine monitor)
items.content: The software that **creates and runs VMs** and **shares the real hardware** between them: it gives each VM a slice of CPU time, a part of RAM (using paging) and a virtual disk, which is just a large file on the host. Examples: **VirtualBox**, **VMware**, **Hyper-V**, **KVM**.

blocks.content: A **system virtual machine** emulates the **whole hardware** of a computer, so a **complete guest operating system** can be installed on it. Examples: running **Linux inside Windows** in VirtualBox to learn the command line; running an old Windows XP program that no longer works on Windows 11; or, in a data centre, running **dozens of virtual servers on one physical server**. This last use is the basis of **cloud computing**: when a company rents a "server" from a cloud provider, it is usually given a virtual machine. The hypervisor keeps the VMs **isolated**: a crash, a misconfiguration or malware inside one VM does not affect the host or the other VMs. A whole VM can be saved as a **snapshot** and restored later, copied to another server or backed up as a single file.

A **process virtual machine** does not emulate a whole computer; it runs **one program** and provides it with a **platform-independent environment**. The best-known example is the **Java Virtual Machine (JVM)**. A Java program is compiled not into the machine code of a particular CPU but into an intermediate code called **bytecode**. Each platform — Windows on x86, macOS on ARM, Linux, Android — has its own JVM, which **translates the bytecode** into the machine code of that computer while the program runs. So the **same compiled program runs on any computer that has a JVM** ("write once, run anywhere"). Other process VMs are the **.NET Common Language Runtime (CLR)**, the **Python** virtual machine that runs Python bytecode, and the **Android Runtime**.
